At the Races: The new Trump Democrats

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
  • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
  • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

“We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

Andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

It has been revealed that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews said, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

“We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” stated Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of Newly introduced York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

“I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

Recent findings suggest that “I respect them,” he stated. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

Sources indicate that peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

Recent findings suggest that A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

#KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, released his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

Recent findings suggest that rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, revealed he aims to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

They’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

In a recent development, RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

In a recent development, where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

Recent findings suggest that thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

Recent findings suggest that battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

Industry observers note that #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun introduced his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but said last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

Fresh leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

Investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

In a recent development, tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, declared a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

The  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

Only the young: Newly introduced York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who notes she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the New York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

After Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

West Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

Recent findings suggest that the last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

Machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

Monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly noted he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

What India Makes of Trump’s Asia Trip

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S.
  • The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S.
  • The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

Sources indicate that the highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan issues a plea for medical treatment.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan concerns a plea for medical treatment.

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday. Australia, India, Japan, and the United States declared initiatives including cybersecurity collaboration, a cable connectivity framework, and a maritime surveillance exercise.

Sources indicate that the Quad meeting likely brought some relief for New Delhi. The grouping is important for India’s foreign-policy interests, bringing together some of its closest security partners in an effort to counter China. (However, the Quad states rarely mention Beijing in their public messaging about the grouping to avoid antagonizing the superpower.).

Sources indicate that though India has engineered a rapprochement with China in the last two years, taking steps to reduce border tensions and scale up trade and investment, they remain bitter strategic rivals. India prioritizes opportunities to work multilaterally to push back against China’s power through non-security collaborations in areas such as technology and infrastructure investment.

According to recent reports, scheduling issues and U.S.-India tensions have prevented high-level Quad engagement since September 2024. Quad supporters will point to Tuesday’s meeting as an indication of the grouping’s resilience, much like how it bounced back from quiescence in 2017—interestingly, with another summit in Manila when each member’s ties with China faced increasing strain.

Industry observers note that still, the Quad remains mired in uncertainty, mainly because of U.S. President Donald Trump. His administration’s signaling about taking a softer approach to competition with China, coupled with silence about the fate of the U.S. Indo-Pacific strategy, suggests that the current White House may not be prepared to throw its full support behind the Quad.

Recent findings suggest that though an incoming Democratic Congress might take a tougher line on China, this is unlikely to shape the Trump administration’s thinking on the Quad. As a result, the wider ASEAN summit arguably held more immediate significance for New Delhi than the Quad meeting.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has long sought to step up India’s game in Southeast Asia—a region home to key Indian partners and multiple growing economies. India has especially strong incentives to ramp up engagement given China’s large footprint there. In that sense, the stakes were high for Modi’s engagement with ASEAN leaders this week.

Newly introduced Delhi will now closely watch as Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a historic trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. There is a lack of clarity, but the discussion will reportedly include the Iran war and nuclear nonproliferation.

Industry observers note that such themes are unlikely to concern India, which has a strong interest in the wars in both Iran and Ukraine coming to an end. But the summit will be a vindication of sorts for Fresh Delhi. In 2025, Trump slammed a meeting among Modi, Xi, and Putin in China; now, he is coming to the same table.

However, the boost that China is likely to get from the trilateral isn’t ideal for India. The U.S., Chinese, and Russian leaders have never had such a formal face-to-face exchange. Beijing’s capacity to convene the three leaders, against a backdrop of long-standing U.S.-Russia hostility, is a major diplomatic achievement.

For Fresh Delhi, the biggest takeaway from this week’s high-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen is that the Quad leaders’ meeting was a relative sideshow. The ASEAN and APEC summits will generate more attention and hold more immediate significance for Indian policymakers.

Bangladesh cleared for DFC investment. The U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC) declared on Monday that Bangladesh was now eligible to receive its financing. The DFC, which mobilizes private investment, has taken on added importance since the demise of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) last year.

Until now, Bangladesh was ineligible for DFC financing because of U.S. concerns about labor conditions in the country. Negotiations between Washington and Dhaka to address these concerns and clear the way go back to the Biden administration.

Sources indicate that the announcement couldn’t come at a better time for Bangladesh, which faces serious development challenges and severe economic stress. Some of its most pressing challenges—such as fuel shortages and the world’s worst measles epidemic—are tied to energy and healthcare, two of DFC’s priority areas for investment.

DFC-funded projects could bring a boost to U.S.-Bangladesh relations. Development cooperation, for years embodied by the large USAID mission in Dhaka, has long been a major component of the relationship.

Sources indicate that khan complications plea for medical treatment. Lawyers for Imran Khan sent an open letter on Monday from the jailed former prime minister to top judges in Pakistan, imploring them to secure better healthcare for Khan and his wife, who is also in prison. In the letter, Khan indicates he is suffering from high blood pressure and is at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

In a recent development, for months, Khan’s lawyers, family, and supporters have said his health is worsening, while officials say he is stable and regularly monitored by prison doctors. In August, Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered Khan to be transferred to a private hospital for an extended period; he was instead brought to a government hospital and only briefly.

In a recent development, concern for Khan’s health was one reason why leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party declared nationwide protests last month. But aside from some demonstrations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the only one governed by the PTI, the campaign didn’t materialize. The party might be back-channeling with the country’s leadership to secure concessions for Khan.

British royals visit India. The United Kingdom’s Prince William and Princess Catherine completed a three-day visit to India on Wednesday. They began their trip in Mumbai, where they participated in the Earthshot Prize ceremony. William founded the award, which focuses on developing fresh solutions to climate change.

Recent findings suggest that the royal couple then traveled to New Delhi, where they met Modi. Their visit underscores the strong ties between India and its former colonizer. U.K.-India relations have deepened in recent years, buoyed most recently by a free trade deal that formally entered into force in July.

Recent findings suggest that for that matter, U.K.-Pakistan ties are also quite warm; William and Kate made a visit there in 2019. Deep people-to-people ties, thanks in part to large Indian and Pakistani diasporas in the U.K., help bolster these relationships. British colonial rule may have left a problematic legacy in the subcontinent, but diplomacy today is in a good place.

According to recent reports, new Delhi hosts an arts and culture forum this weekend under the banner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). The idea for the Civilisational Dialogue Forum came from India, which will head the event even though Pakistan is the current SCO chair. Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, will travel to New Delhi to represent Islamabad.

With India-Pakistan ties so tense in recent years, the rare occasions when senior ministers from one country have traveled to the other have mostly come in their capacity as SCO members.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari traveled to India for an SCO summit in 2023, while Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar went to Pakistan the next year. Malik’s visit, however, comes at an especially fraught moment, with the relationship essentially frozen since the brief military conflict between India and Pakistan in 2025.

Looking ahead, a big question is whether Modi will travel to Pakistan for the SCO leaders’ summit scheduled for next August. Modi visited Pakistan in December 2015, early in his first term. Several days after his trip, Pakistani terrorists attacked an Indian Air Force base. Since that incident, Modi’s government has taken an especially hard line toward Pakistan.

Even though Jaishankar went to Pakistan in 2024, it is unlikely that Modi himself will make the trip next year—especially if the protest movement against his government that has gripped India in recent months remains active.

In the Daily Mirror, writer K.K.S. Perera analyzes Sri Lanka’s upcoming budget: “Has the 2027 Budget adequately addressed the economic difficulties confronting ordinary Sri Lankans? The answer must be examined against people’s actual living conditions rather than the Government’s financial projections, development promises, and announcements.”.

Sources indicate that in the Print, education expert Archana Dalmia reflects on Italian-born Indian politician Sonia Gandhi’s newly introduced memoir, Belonging. “Destiny had written a very different story from the one she could ever have imagined,” she writes. “Through love, loss and the unexpected turns of life, she became part of a country that was once so distant from her own.”.

In Dawn, public health specialist Muhammad Aftab Gohar argues the urgency of eliminating rabies in Pakistan. “The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030,” he writes. “A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.”.

A New Kind of Foreign Agent

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.
  • Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding.
  • In a recent development, like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.

Foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a newly introduced type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.

In a recent development, like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.

Recent findings suggest that although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.

FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.).

In a recent development, today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No new statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.

Recent findings suggest that democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.

American AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.

By law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.

Industry observers note that that is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”.

Industry observers note that but these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. People rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.

Although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.

Recent findings suggest that these models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.

In a recent development, chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI firm Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere said it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when users asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”.

Despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.

American companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its latest model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese company Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.

Recent findings suggest that although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a firm uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.

In terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.

Although AI is a newly introduced technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI company acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.

Beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a tech giant can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”.

Sources indicate that for FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.

After registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.

All content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to update them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”.

In a recent development, the standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media company disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.

American companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the company serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”.

In the first, an American manufacturer takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political issues with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.

In the second scenario, an American firm outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should revision its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”.

American companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI tech giant, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research shows that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should glitch standards on how to train away FARA liability.

Although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department states it is considering a fresh rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.

Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.

FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.

Unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.

In a recent development, every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical organization can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.

According to recent reports, by welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
  • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
  • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

Industry observers note that “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., said earlier this year.

The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

“We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., stated during the meeting.

When former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

Sources indicate that “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

Industry observers note that the committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

Sources indicate that it comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

“The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she said in a statement earlier this week.

Cammack noted that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

“Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

Ethics ranking member Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., stated everyone in the House should have “zero tolerance” for sexual harassment.

“We’ve worked very hard to look at ways that we could make the committee’s process fair, transparent and accountable, and I think we’ve done that,” he said at Thursday’s meeting.

  • In a recent development, so keen was the Philippines to have U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two new trade deals in the region.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two latest trade deals in the region.

In a recent development, so keen was the Philippines to have U.S. President Donald Trump attend the annual leader’s summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) that it changed the dates just for him. Originally scheduled to run five days earlier, it was shifted to run Nov. 15 through Nov. 17, the better to accommodate the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which is running yesterday and today in Shenzhen, China.

Industry observers note that ASEAN can also take pleasure in the fact that Trump has now attended two years running. Under previous administrations, the nonattendance of the U.S. president or senior U.S. officials was a running complaint.

Sources indicate that after all the hoopla, then, what did the visit add up to? Not much, it seems.

Last year, when Kuala Lumpur hosted, the world was still gripped by questions about tariff negotiations. And Trump also got to play the peacemaker between Thailand and Cambodia—even though fighting between the two resumed the next month.

It has been revealed that this time, no single matter defined the U.S. president’s visit, which lasted less than 24 hours. Trump proclaimed that the United States and Philippines had signed their biggest “ever” trade deal. But in typical Trump style, few details were forthcoming and nothing has actually been signed.

On a symbolic level for Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Trump’s arrival is a nice sign of the continued close relationship between the two countries.

According to recent reports, manila’s previous president, Rodrigo Duterte, was deeply skeptical of the United States, flirting with ending the two countries’ alliance in favor of a deal with China. Marcos has spun the other way, doubling down on the security relationship with Washington to push back against Beijing.

A few other deliverables were also duly delivered upon.

In a recent development, A set of deals involving anti-scam initiatives was finalized. A “trade deal” with Thailand—which, like the Philippines deal, was not actually a final agreement—was announced.

Recent findings suggest that the leaders of the other Quad countries—Australia, Japan, and India—got a grand total of 55 scheduled minutes with Trump. The announcements that came out of that mainly repackaged old agreements.

And Marcos arranged for some food from Jollibee—the Philippines’ top fast-food chain and a national icon—to be delivered to Trump in the interest of “providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do.”.

Sources indicate that at the state dinner, where Jollibee was not served, the U.S. president delivered a typically Trumpian speech. He assured ASEAN that he would support “partners and allies 100 percent,” adding that “when there’s a problem, you’ll call me.”.

He also took the opportunity to praise Marcos for his “very good genetics” as well as calling on Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto to stand up for compliments.

According to recent reports, some had expected announcements on Pax Silica, the United States’ global AI initiative. The United States is planning to build enormous semiconductor and data center facilities on land that used to house one of its military bases in the Philippines. But no announcements were forthcoming.

The Philippine government is keen on the idea as a way to boost its chips and electronics industry, as well as develop its defense industrial base. But the project is also controversial, spurring worries about the environmental impact and displacement of local people.

According to recent reports, protesters took to the streets over Trump’s arrival to make their displeasure heard. Police reacted by blocking marches and detaining people. Nearly 300 demonstrators were arrested, according to protest organizers.

According to recent reports, don’t read too much into this, though. The Philippines is one of the few countries in the world where Trump is still popular. A poll by Pew Research Centre found that 68 percent of Filipinos trusted Trump to do the right thing, the highest of any country surveyed.

Sources indicate that overshadowing all of this was Trump’s next set of meetings in Shenzhen. Will he meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in a trilateral with Chinese President Xi Jinping? Maybe. Will he meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un? Also maybe.

Industry observers note that so—at the end of the day—did Trump just stop by Manila for a pit stop, a photo op, and some Filipino fried food? Maybe.

Not yet… Myanmar isn’t back in ASEAN, yet. Despite determined lobbying from Thailand, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing still wasn’t invited to attend the ASEAN summit.

According to recent reports, since its 2021 coup, ASEAN has expressed its displeasure with Myanmar by not allowing junta leaders to attend summits. Senior civil servants get sent instead.

However, a leaders’ statement adopted on Sunday declared that ASEAN would pursue “calibrated engagement with Myanmar” and “may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation.”.

The widespread assumption is that come 2028, when Thailand is the chair of the bloc, the final barriers will be removed.

The argument for reengagement is that, like it or not, the junta is there. Therefore, ASEAN countries need to engage—especially Thailand, which shares more than 2,000 kilometers of border with Myanmar.

Sources indicate that critics will counter that engagement doesn’t seem to yield much. After the ASEAN summit, Min Aung Hlaing went on a rant in which he mentioned that the statement on Myanmar was unreasonable. He also accused three unnamed member states of prejudice.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, in late October, fighting between junta forces and rebel groups on the Myanmar-Thia border saw explosives and shrapnel spill over to the Thai side. One Thai woman was wounded, and buildings were damaged.

Not quite… The draft “Code of Conduct on the South China Sea,” which the Philippines pushed so hard for, wasn’t finished. According to Marcos in his press conference at the end of the summit, it’s 85 percent done, and all that’s left is the defining of terms.

Sources indicate that with the actual terms as yet unknown, there is, on the summit sidelines, a good deal of cynicism. Even if the agreement is finished next year, many see two decidedly nonthrilling options.

Industry observers note that one is that in order for China to sign the agreement, it will have to be extremely thin, with little fresh or binding terms in it. Second, if some reasonable guidelines are set out, China will just ignore them when it suits it.

An analyst from a country with its own big claim on the waters suggested to me that a code of conduct could even be a disadvantage. If China breaks the rules, then other more rule-abiding countries might find their options to respond constrained by the agreement.

Not on the agenda… Remember the Thailand-Cambodia conflict? ASEAN doesn’t, it seems.

Following last summer’s fighting, ASEAN made an effort to address it. A Trump-sponsored peace deal was signed at the summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Following renewed fighting in December, an ASEAN observer team was unveiled. And in Cebu, Philippines, earlier this year, the two countries met on the sidelines for Philippine-brokered talks, even if the results were limited.

Industry observers note that this time around? Not a squeak. Partly to blame is perhaps that Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet didn’t attend. He was in Phnom Penh hosting the Francophonie Summit—see below.

Sources indicate that sorry for the secondhand smoke. During the ASEAN summit, Prabowo apologized to Malaysia and Singapore for how they have been affected by the haze from Indonesia’s vast forest fires last month.

He then rather undercut it by adding, “It is not our fault, but once again we apologize.”.

Sources indicate that singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also proposed that ASEAN should establish a joint task force to probe companies linked to such fires. This would expand on the current bilateral Singapore-Indonesia task force established last month following some diplomatic spats on the topic.

Trade deals. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney dropped by on Saturday for the announcement that two trade deals were nearly done. Both an ASEAN-Canada and a Canada-Philippines trade deal have been forged with the aim of getting both signed next year.

How much free trade will actually be in these agreements? It’s hard to tell with no text published, but past experience suggests that any changes will probably be more incremental than sweeping.

Wow, everything’s computer. On Saturday, ASEAN signed its Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which should come into force in early 2027. The proclaimed aim is to create an “interconnected ASEAN digital marketplace.”.

It has been revealed that what does this mean in practice? The text’s not out yet, but this Singaporean government announcement lays out some broad strokes—mainly, accepting electronic trade documents, clearer rules on cross-border data flows, and a guarantee of no taxes on them for now, as well as cooperation on artificial intelligence and financial technology.

Recent findings suggest that oil stockpile. Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, and Thailand agreed to set up shared stockpiles of diesel and gasoline to help manage future energy crises. The actual facilities will be built in Indonesia and Thailand.

Industry observers note that laos’s contestant, Thinla (center), performs during the grand final of the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 at One Bangkok Forum in Bangkok on Nov. 14.Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP via Getty Images.

Recent findings suggest that cambodia: Cambodia hosted the Francophonie Summit from Saturday to Monday, gathering countries from across the French-speaking world—loosely defined. Prime Minister Hun Manet skipped ASEAN for this event and used it to do some diplomatic lobbying for Cambodia over its border dispute with Thailand, which infuriated the Thai government. French President Emmanuel Macron called for the investigation of the killing of a former opposition lawmaker and French Cambodian dual citizen Lim Kimya in Bangkok in 2025.

Indonesia: Police raided a data center owned by Megaspeed and found empty server racks. Prabowo is expected to pick a loyalist from his own party to be the next VP. Online phenomenon iShowSpeed indicated off his Indonesian-speaking skills at an awards ceremony and then on a phone call with former U.S. President Barack Obama. And Nikkei has published a great article on Indonesia’s runners-for-hire who will burnish your Strava for you.

In a recent development, malaysia: The governing coalition faced another setback with a loss in the Melaka state election. And Macron visited on Tuesday and pitched cooperation on rare earths, weapons, semiconductors, and nuclear energy to reduce dependence on the United States and China.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, mentioned additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

According to recent reports, the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

“When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

Recent findings suggest that as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

It has been revealed that as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

Last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

It has been revealed that “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, mentioned at a news conference.

Industry observers note that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office said in a news release.

According to recent reports, “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

“Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., said Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

As with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

The resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

Recent findings suggest that john M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.
