Tech Report: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3970 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
  • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
  • According to recent reports, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

According to recent reports, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

It has been revealed that yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

In recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

It has been revealed that at the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

The success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

International efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

It has been revealed that in the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

According to recent reports, there is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France declared the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

Sources indicate that simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

The integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

According to recent reports, together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will swiftly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

According to recent reports, in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

According to recent reports, but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

According to recent reports, wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

Sources indicate that war also creates upcoming dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

Recent findings suggest that finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to latest waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

The world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

It has been revealed that but it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

Spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Industry observers note that deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

Countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

Industry observers note that investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

In a recent development, yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

Recent findings suggest that reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

Industry observers note that the twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

All of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

Recent findings suggest that strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

Sources indicate that the first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An patch to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly vital, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The upcoming seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats presently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

Permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

In a recent development, another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral Latest START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

It has been revealed that yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

In a recent development, technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

In a recent development, the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

It has been revealed that proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a new UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

Halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

According to recent reports, ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

International financial institutions must be able to deliver financing rapidly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

Recent findings suggest that this is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, introduced with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

Industry observers note that A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

#88560. Industry News: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab

Industry News: How a $1B Obama-era solar plant went bankrupt twice, leaving taxpayers with the tab

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foxnews

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicist and energy researcher Oliver Hemmers explains the engineering failures and economic challenges behind the collapse of Nevada’s billion-dollar Crescent Dunes solar plant.
  • — An Obama-era solar power plant once hailed as a "clean energy marvel" and backed by more than $1 billion in federal support has gone bankrupt for a second time and sold for just $7 million — with the estimated taxpayer tab potentially reaching $507.6 million.
  • Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicist and energy researcher Oliver Hemmers explains the engineering failures and economic challenges behind the collapse of Nevada’s billion-dollar Crescent Dunes solar plant.

TONOPAH, Nev. — An Obama-era solar power plant once hailed as a "clean energy marvel" and backed by more than $1 billion in federal support has gone bankrupt for a second time and sold for just $7 million — with the estimated taxpayer tab potentially reaching $507.6 million.

Rising from the barren Nevada desert, the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project looks like a futuristic fortress in a vast, dusty wasteland, with more than 10,000 mirrors surrounding a giant central tower. The plant was designed to generate solar electricity even after sunset, using an emerging technology that promised to revolutionize green energy in America.

The Obama administration bet big on the project, backing it with a $737 million federal loan guarantee and around $275 million in Treasury grant awards as part of its broader $90 billion push to combat climate change and stimulate the economy following the 2008 financial crisis.

OBAMA-ERA 'CLEAN ENERGY' SOLAR POWER PLANT STILL USES FOSSIL FUELS – AND KILLS THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY.

The Crescent Dunes solar plant's central tower is shown unlit, left, and illuminated by reflected sunlight, right. The Obama-era project, backed by more than $1 billion in federal support, went bankrupt twice before selling for $7 million in July 2026. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital (left); Getty Images (right).).

But the promise never matched the performance.

After operations began in late 2015, leaks and equipment failures repeatedly knocked the plant offline, production fell short and cheaper solar alternatives undercut its economics — driving the project into financial ruin and leaving taxpayers shouldering the cost.

The financial collapse comes 15 years after Solyndra, another Obama-backed solar firm, went bankrupt and left taxpayers in the red for $528 million — a sum Crescent Dunes' estimated taxpayer tab could nearly match.

In a recent development, "The Crescent Dunes solar project is a microcosm of what is wrong with Democrat governance: the Green Newly introduced Scam, hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars wasted, fraud, and a cover-up," Rep. Lance Gooden, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital.

OBAMA-BACKED $2.2B GREEN ENERGY 'BOONDOGGLE' LEAVES TAXPAYERS ON THE HOOK.

Recent findings suggest that president Barack Obama signs the $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act as Vice President Joe Biden looks on in Denver, Colorado, on Feb. 17, 2009. The legislation helped finance the Obama administration's push into renewable energy, including the federal loan program that backed the Crescent Dunes solar project in Nevada. (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images).

Crescent Dunes sits about 13 miles northwest of the old mining town of Tonopah, roughly halfway between Las Vegas and Reno.

The isolated facility, which Fox News Digital toured, is surrounded by miles of barren desert, scrubland and distant mountain ranges.

Across the 2,250-acre federal site, more than 10,000 giant mirrors surround a 640-foot tower — the centerpiece of a system designed to overcome one of solar power's biggest limitations: darkness.

According to recent reports, unlike ordinary solar panels, which convert sunlight directly into electricity, Crescent Dunes focuses the sun's rays onto a receiver atop the tower, heating molten salt to roughly 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit. The salt stores that heat in a massive insulated tank, allowing it to produce steam that drives an electricity-generating turbine long after sunset.

In a recent development, that combination made it the first commercial-scale U.S. solar tower to use molten salt to both collect and store the sun's heat. DOE projected it would generate 482,000 megawatt-hours annually, with a maximum output of 110 megawatts — enough to supply more than 75,000 Nevada homes during peak periods.

The Crescent Dunes solar plant uses more than 10,000 mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a central receiver, heating molten salt that stores energy. The stored heat is used to produce steam, drive a turbine and generate electricity, including after sunset. (Fox News).

SolarReserve, ACS Group/Cobra and Banco Santander were original project participants in Crescent Dunes, which received a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee and approximately $275.6 million in Treasury grant awards. CMB investors also provided $90 million in private financing. (Fox News).

American developer SolarReserve developed the project, while Spanish contractor Cobra, a subsidiary of construction giant ACS Group, built it.

Both held ownership stakes in the company that owned the plant, Tonopah Solar Energy.

Spanish banking giant Banco Santander also held an ownership stake in Tonopah Solar Energy.

Industry observers note that then-Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nev., championed the project. In 2016, he called it an "engineering and clean energy marvel" and predicted that "Nevada will benefit for decades.".

The project reflected the Obama administration's push to expand clean energy by using taxpayer-backed financing to help bring promising but commercially risky technologies to market.

But Crescent Dunes demonstrated how expensive those gambles could become when they failed.

Crescent Dunes' problems emerged almost immediately.

A major leak in its molten-salt storage tank occurred in October 2016 — less than a year after commercial operations began.

During that shutdown, Treasury approved a cash-grant payment in March 2017 under the Obama-era stimulus program — funding that later became the subject of serious fraud allegations.

It went back online in July 2017, but restarting the plant did not resolve its performance problems.

Even in 2018, its best full year through 2025, Crescent Dunes generated just 41% of the annual electricity output projected by DOE, according to federal energy records.

Then another tank failure halted generation in March 2019.

Seven months later, the repeated breakdowns and poor performance eventually cost Crescent Dunes its sole electricity customer when NV Energy terminated its 25-year agreement.

Without its long-term power contract, Crescent Dunes spiraled into financial trouble, culminating in its first bankruptcy in July 2020.

The 2020 restructuring handed ownership to ACS through its affiliate, Crescent Dunes Investment, with Cobra running the plant. The turnaround plan counted on extensive repairs restoring production to 400,000 megawatt-hours a year — more than twice its best annual output.

Recent findings suggest that the hot molten-salt storage tank at Crescent Dunes in Nevada. Repeated leaks involving the plant's molten-salt storage system contributed to lengthy shutdowns and financial troubles. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

A network of pipes and industrial equipment forms part of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The concentrated solar plant uses molten salt to capture and store heat before using it to generate steam and electricity. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

The plant restarted in July 2021, only for further molten-salt-tank leaks in 2022 and 2023 to force additional shutdowns.

Although the plant resumed selling electricity under shorter-term agreements, it continued to lose money and relied on financial support from affiliated companies, court records show.

REGULATORS ALLOW OBAMA-ERA SOLAR PLANT TO KILL THOUSANDS OF BIRDS ANNUALLY, INVESTIGATION FINDS.

By January 2026, it was back in bankruptcy court. This time, the billion-dollar plant went on the auction block.

Mississippi-based Sons of Liberty Construction, a company owned by three brothers, bought it for $7 million in July and are attempting to revive it.

The plant was generating electricity during Fox News Digital's visit, although they said it remained well below its initial intended output. Their efforts to restore the troubled facility are examined in Part 3 of this series.

A timeline of the Crescent Dunes solar plant shows major equipment failures in 2016, 2019, 2022 and 2023, along with federal financing, Treasury grant approval, two bankruptcies and the project's eventual $7 million sale in July 2026. (Fox News).

Behind that history of breakdowns and bankruptcies lies a dispute over what failed: the solar technology, the construction behind it, or a combination of both.

Bill Gould, SolarReserve's co-founder and former chief technology officer, blamed the project's Spanish construction contractor, ACS Cobra.

"It was a tragedy of mismanagement," Gould told Bloomberg in 2020, accusing the contractor of delaying necessary work and designing a defective molten-salt tank.

According to recent reports, an unnamed engineer who remarked he had worked at Crescent Dunes since its early development offered a similar account, blaming the tank failures on design and welding problems. He told SolarPACES in 2023 that the plant's solar collection technology had experienced comparatively few problems.

"It's just the old tech that's having these troubles," the engineer remarked, referring to the conventional thermal-power equipment.

The sheer size of the storage system posed a significant challenge, according to Oliver Hemmers, a physicist and energy researcher who formerly led the Harry Reid Center for Environmental Studies at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

"Ultimately, the larger you make those tanks that hold the molten salt, the harder the material science challenges become," Hemmers told Fox News Digital.

Hemmers mentioned temperature swings of hundreds of degrees can cause the metal to repeatedly expand and contract, eventually creating cracks and leaks. He had not reviewed the plant's engineering aims but questioned whether the developers had sufficiently tested the tank design.

"You need to have alloys that can withstand that heat variation without moving much. Otherwise, when the walls move, the vessel breaks, cracks and leaks. So I'm not sure how much research they really put into the vessel design," he remarked.

Hemmers noted that Crescent Dunes relied on a massive molten-salt storage tank, while other solar thermal facilities have used multiple smaller tanks to reduce the stresses caused by repeated heating and cooling.

Court records show how efforts to prevent further failures came at a cost.

According to recent reports, when the plant resumed operations in July 2023, operators lowered the hot-salt tank's temperature from its original design level of about 1,050 degrees Fahrenheit to about 850 degrees. They later raised it to as high as 900 degrees, but the lower temperatures still reduced electricity production and revenue.

Industry observers note that A 2015 Department of Energy promotional poster touts the Crescent Dunes solar project in Nevada, highlighting its $737 million federal loan guarantee and projected annual electricity generation of 482,000 megawatt-hours. The plant later suffered repeated equipment failures and two bankruptcies before being sold for $7 million in 2026. (U.S. Department of Energy).

The receiver atop the 640-foot solar tower at Crescent Dunes glows as mirrors concentrate sunlight onto it near Tonopah, Nevada, in August 2026. The troubled plant was sold for $7 million following its second bankruptcy earlier that year. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

As Crescent Dunes struggled to meet its production targets, competing solar technology was getting cheaper.

Falling prices for conventional solar panels, known as photovoltaic panels, including those manufactured in China, undercut the project.

Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity, offering a simpler and increasingly cheaper way to generate solar power.

Industry observers note that crescent Dunes, by contrast, uses more than 10,000 computer-controlled mirrors, called heliostats, to focus sunlight onto a receiver atop its central tower. The heat warms molten salt, which is then used to produce steam that drives turbines to generate electricity.

According to recent reports, the mirrored faces of heliostats at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto a receiver atop the plant's central tower, heating molten salt used to store thermal energy. (Michael Dorgan).

Crescent Dunes, however, has one key advantage: Its molten-salt storage system allows it to generate electricity even after sunset, something conventional solar panels cannot do without additional storage.

According to recent reports, those same economic pressures have battered California's Ivanpah solar plant, another Obama-era project Fox News Digital reported on that uses thousands of heliostats to concentrate sunlight. Unlike Crescent Dunes, Ivanpah cannot store the sun's heat to generate electricity after dark.

Fox News Digital contacted ACS Group and its attorneys but received no response.

The project was backed by more than $1 billion in federal loan guarantees and grants.

That included a $737 million Department of Energy loan guarantee. DOE said it resolved its financial interests in the project through the plant's first bankruptcy settlement in 2020 in an effort to maximize taxpayer recovery and estimated its loss on the loan at $232 million — a figure the department confirmed to Fox News Digital on background.

The Trump administration's Department of Energy blasted the handling of taxpayer money behind the project.

"It is unfortunate that previous administrations irresponsibly managed taxpayer dollars in their support of the Green Newly introduced Scam. Since 2020, DOE has had no ownership, operational, or financial interest in the Obama-era project," DOE assistant press secretary Caroline Murzin told Fox News Digital in a written statement.

The project also received a $275.6 million Treasury grant award, which, unlike the loan, was not intended to be repaid provided the project met the program's requirements.

Combined, the Treasury grant awards and DOE's estimated loan loss would put the total federal cost at approximately $507.6 million, although Treasury has not confirmed the full grant was disbursed and DOE has not provided a final accounting of its loan losses.

Fox News Digital has filed Freedom of Information Act requests with both the Energy and Treasury departments seeking a full accounting of the federal loans, grant payments and taxpayer losses associated with Crescent Dunes.

Rows of computer-controlled heliostats surround the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The mirrors track the sun and direct concentrated sunlight toward the receiver atop the tower. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

A view looking up at the receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada, while the receiver is not being illuminated by concentrated sunlight. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Sources indicate that the Treasury grant also became the focus of a private investor-backed lawsuit alleging that companies involved in construction fraudulently secured the money. A judge dismissed the case at DOJ's request and the investors are appealing.

The allegations and the fight over the dismissal are examined in Part 2.

Reid, who died in 2021, had championed Crescent Dunes as a showcase for government and private industry working together to build "the next generation of clean energy technology.".

Its financial collapse has sharpened the question behind that partnership: Should taxpayers bankroll commercially risky energy projects that private lenders are unwilling to fully finance?

"The government shouldn't be picking winners and losers," Véronique de Rugy, an economist at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, told Fox News Digital.

In a recent development, "This is not the role of the government. The government is not good at actually picking projects that somehow the private sector is leaving on the sidewalk," she said.

Former President Barack Obama, right, is pictured alongside the Crescent Dunes solar plant in Nevada, left. The Obama-era project received more than $1 billion in federal backing before going bankrupt twice and selling for $7 million in July 2026. The images are a composite. (Taylor Hill/Getty Images).

De Rugy argued that politicians take credit for publicly financed projects without facing the same consequences when they collapse. Unlike private investors, she remarked, politicians don't personally bear the financial losses when their bets go wrong.

"So then they can go and do a ribbon cutting ceremony when the plant opens, and then they're usually nowhere to be seen when the organization goes under," she remarked.

She also argued that many companies receiving government assistance would have succeeded without it, questioning why taxpayers should shoulder the risks of commercial investments.

"These subsidies go to projects that end up failing, right, then taxpayers have to shoulder the bill," she said.

Nick Loris, president of the Conservative Coalition for Climate Solutions (C3 Solutions), a conservative energy and environmental policy think tank, offered a different perspective, arguing that government financing can sometimes justify the risks of developing fresh technologies.

Recent findings suggest that "I wouldn't call it a mistake. I think it took a risky bet on a potentially promising technology that aimed to solve one of the challenges with solar in its intermittency," Loris told Fox News Digital.

He argued that federal financing can help promising technologies reach the market when private investors are reluctant to take the risk, and that failures such as Crescent Dunes should be weighed against successful projects and interest earnings across DOE's broader loan portfolio.

It has been revealed that one example is California's Desert Sunlight, a 550-megawatt solar farm that uses panels instead of mirrors and molten salt. In a 2024 assessment, DOE said the project helped prove the viability of large-scale solar and was meeting its loan obligations.

Across the broader program, DOE reported in its fiscal 2027 budget justification that borrowers had paid nearly $5 billion in interest, compared with nearly $1 billion in default losses, through Sept. 30, 2025.

But Hemmers questioned whether Crescent Dunes ever made economic sense, arguing that the billion-dollar investment was a risky gamble from the outset.

"Right, we kind of say, okay, that was a boondoggle. It didn't work. And so now we move on, right, do something else," Hemmers remarked.

Asked whether Crescent Dunes deserved that label, he doubled down.

"I think so, yeah. I think from the get-go, it started off too expensive, and I think it was unfortunate, let's say for the developer, that they run into all these technical problems on top of it," he mentioned.

"And as we can see from that project, it completely failed in the end.".

In a recent development, A close-up view of one of more than 10,000 heliostats at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. Each structure consists of multiple mirrors mounted on a computer-controlled system that tracks the sun. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

According to recent reports, concentrated sunlight illuminates the receiver atop the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project's tower near Tonopah, Nevada. Molten salt is pumped through the receiver and heated before returning to a storage tank at ground level. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Electrical equipment and transmission infrastructure at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

A welcome sign greets visitors to Tonopah, Nevada, a historic mining town roughly 13 miles southeast of the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

Industry observers note that rows of computer-controlled heliostats lead toward the glowing receiver tower at the Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project near Tonopah, Nevada. The mirrors concentrate sunlight onto the receiver, where molten salt is heated and used to store thermal energy. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, left, and Mitch McConnell , R-Ky., won't be smiling as much if Democrats force a punt on spending bills to next year. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Recent findings suggest that newly released Senate appropriations bills would distribute $8.7 billion in "congressionally directed spending" secured by 78 senators for their home states — earmarked dollars that could disappear if Congress resorts to a stopgap funding measure to avert a partial government shutdown after Dec. 11.

Nearly 4,000 individual earmarks are contained in nine of the 12 draft fiscal 2027 spending bills, a CQ Roll Call tally found; the remaining three bills — Defense, State-Foreign Operations and Legislative Branch — don't have any.

According to recent reports, there's typically some overlap between House and Senate projects that would get weeded out in final negotiations to avoid duplication. But for comparison's sake, House Republicans included nearly 6,700 line items worth $8.2 billion in their earmarked spending bills.

Democrats have signaled they'll push for a continuing resolution into the first quarter of next year enabling them to rewrite the full-year fiscal 2027 bills when they take the gavels in January, possibly upping the overall pot of earmarked funds — or at least divvying up the pie more favorably to blue states and districts.

But that would mean the final attempt by departing lawmakers like Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, and longtime Senate GOP leader and senior appropriator Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, to deliver for their states might be all for naught.

And top Democrats with substantial earmarking success under GOP governance, such as Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash., will have to start from scratch.

Here are some key stats on senators' earmarks in the latest batch of spending bills Collins is trying to get across the finish line.

Naturally, much of the spoils go to Senate Appropriations Committee members, and that's no different this year. But with so many more Democrats requesting projects — often jointly with their fellow delegation member — individual contributions may appear diluted given they have to share the credit.

According to recent reports, that dilution shows up in the rankings when allocating credit in a way that avoids double-counting — everyone gets an equal share of his or her joint projects, so $20 million sponsored jointly by two senators will appear as $10 million for each. Solo earmarkers in this scenario face no such dilution.

Using the even-split methodology, the top 10 — all senior appropriators — look like this:.

Another way to look at it is by simply adding up every instance of a senator affixing his or her name to a project, which leads to double-counting but gives them full credit for every earmark secured, even with jointly requested projects.

Here's the top 10 in that scenario:.

Finally, there's the solo earmarker leaderboard, only counting dollars secured without any co-sponsors:.

McConnell and Collins hit the trifecta, ending up among the top three in all three scenarios.

Related: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks.

Unlike the House, where states with the largest populations receive the most funding by virtue of having more representatives securing earmarks, smaller states punch above their weight in the Senate — particularly when their delegations achieve exalted positions of seniority.

Hence Washington state — with Murray and Cantwell, the Commerce Committee ranking member, representing it — is way out in front.

By contrast, the second- and third-most populous states — Texas and Florida — received a grand total of zero earmarked funds, because their GOP senators didn't request any. California, with the largest population, is No. 16 in the ranks; Latest York is 12th.

Here are the top 10 states by earmarked funds procured in the Senate bills, clearly skewing toward smaller, typically reddish states:.

According to recent reports, the Transportation-HUD spending bill continues to be the go-to place for earmarks, accounting for 27 percent of all individual projects in the Senate bills and about one-third of all the earmarked dollars. The next-closest bill, Labor-HHS-Education, has half the earmarked amount that the "T-HUD" bill does.

Top agencies and programs with earmarked funds are housed within, that's right, the departments of Transportation and Housing and Urban Development, with HUD leading the pack thanks to its ever-popular Community Development Fund accounting for all of that department's earmarks.

Recent findings suggest that transportation isn't far behind, thanks largely to highway projects, followed by Health and Human Services and its Health Resources and Services Administration account, which funds community health centers. Defense Department military construction projects and the Army Corps of Engineers round out the group of $1 billion-plus agencies.

Here are the top accounts for earmarked funds in this year's crop of bills:.

The biggest individual earmarks are largely within Army Corps accounts funded in the draft Energy-Water bill, with some military construction and transportation projects and two mega NIST-based university construction earmarks thrown in on behalf of Collins and McConnell.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.

Still, all three will be pleased with the pictures. U.S. President Donald Trump, smarting from his party’s overwhelming defeat in the midterm elections, gets to play statesman. Russian President Vladimir Putin gets to play peacemaker. And Chinese President Xi Jinping gets to play the man in charge—though nowadays that may be more accurate than not.

The official joint statement from the summit, issued by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, echoed themes that Xi has promoted throughout Trump’s second term: strategic stability, opposition to Cold War thinking and economic decoupling, and respect for the outcomes of World War II.

In a recent development, china and Russia routinely trot out that final point to justify their territorial claims today. The irony is rich for China, which was represented during the war by leaders of the Republic of China government, who later fled to Taiwan. (In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, the victorious power was the Soviet Union, not Russia.).

Before the meeting, there was talk that the Shenzhen trilateral might amount to a fresh Yalta Conference—the 1945 summit at which the three main victors of World War II divided up Europe.

This speculation drew on the long-simmering idea that the world might once again be carved into spheres of influence. But the idea that a fresh Yalta is possible at all is fundamentally misguided. Two of the three great powers today are bogged down in economically devastating wars of choice against smaller countries.

Crucially, it is clear that the world is not theirs to divide. Trump cannot force Ukraine to surrender or hand Taiwan to Beijing. Putin cannot restore Soviet grandeur by force. And China, for all its bluster, has yet to bring Taiwan to heel.

The Yalta fantasy also ignores how much weaker today’s great powers are than their 1945 counterparts. At the time, the Soviet military was the largest in the world, the U.S. economy was bigger than those of the rest of the developed world combined, and the diminished United Kingdom still ruled an empire that encompassed one-quarter of the global population.

Sources indicate that nor did the Yalta bargain of a world divided among superpowers hold. Rather than securing a lasting peace, it laid the groundwork for the Cold War and spawned bloodshed from Korea to Hungary within a few years. A grand bargain among China, Russia, and the United States today is even less likely to work.

Industry observers note that for all the talk of a new world order, the summit produced little of substance. The three powers nominally agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but with no advance diplomatic work and significant differences among their arsenals, not much will come of it.

The joint statement did have one effect, though. The leaders’ condemnation of the International Criminal Court handed China and Russia ideological ammunition, reinforcing the autocratic disdain for international institutions and human rights that all countries are meant to uphold.

But Beijing should not mistake the summit for a license to keep the terms of U.S.-China talks strictly about power. With Democrats set to take control of key China-related committees in the U.S. Congress in January, complications involving democracy and political dissidents will take on renewed importance, no matter what Trump or Xi would prefer.

According to recent reports, takaichi receives cold welcome. Hosting the APEC gathering gave China another opportunity to signal its displeasure with Japan. The bilateral relationship is still at a nadir, more than a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi noted a Chinese invasion of Taiwan could justify Japanese intervention.

As other leaders were greeted with fanfare, Takaichi was received at Shenzhen’s airport by a relatively low-ranking diplomat. I suspect there was also implicit misogyny at play: Chinese state media has denigrated Takaichi in sexist terms, as it did with former Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen.

Though Takaichi was largely sidelined at the APEC meeting, she did what she could to meet bilaterally with other leaders instead.

According to recent reports, A magisterial China resource. Last month, scholar Endymion Wilkinson published the eighth edition of Chinese History: A New Manual, one of the most key books in the field of China studies. First published in 1973 as a relatively slim research guide of around 70,000 words, it now approaches 2 million and covers everything from Chinese cuisine to politics.

Wilkinson is now 85, but each latest edition still contains substantial revisions and additions. The latest includes personal recollections from his stints in China: first as an English teacher at Peking University on the eve of the Cultural Revolution and later as the European Union’s ambassador from 1994 to 2001.

A remarkable work of erudition and dedication, the book remains a starting point for virtually any research into China.

Recent findings suggest that nvidia scandal updates. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s marital infidelities continues to widen, with the company facing legal scrutiny and a wider crackdown on U.S. chip exports. Huang had an affair with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang; he resigned from his role last week and is set to testify before the U.S. Congress early next month.

In a recent development, reporting suggests that Nvidia’s involvement in networks designed to evade U.S. export controls lies somewhere between active complicity and willful blindness. Alice Huang’s husband, who reportedly knew about the affair, also played a major part in building state-backed data centers designed to give China access to more computing power.

Alice Huang is now back in Beijing, beyond the reach of potential criminal charges in Singapore.

U.S. cybersecurity risks? As many tech services seemed to break in the last week, many people asked whether the outages were an ordinary screwup or a cyberattack. The consensus so far is that the problems were unrelated, caused by companies rushing to upgrade systems before the holidays.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s worth remembering that China achieved deep penetration of U.S. infrastructure with Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group, which was publicly exposed in 2024. The Trump administration dismantled the expert groups investigating Volt Typhoon early last year, and China could likely still shut down large parts of U.S. life if it chose to do so.
